claim: fMRI is based on the blood-oxygenation-level-dependent (BOLD) contrast mechanism.
source: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is based on the blood-oxygenation-level-dependent (BOLD) contrast mechanism (Ogawa et al., 1990)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ogawa et al., 1990, which is a foundational reference for the BOLD mechanism.

claim: fMRI is widely viewed as the gold standard for studying brain function because of its high spatial resolution and non-invasive nature.
source: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is based on the blood-oxygenation-level-dependent (BOLD) contrast mechanism (Ogawa et al., 1990), and is widely viewed as the gold standard for studying brain function because of its high spatial resolution and non-invasive nature.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the advantages of fMRI.

claim: The BOLD signal exhibits low frequency (~0.01–0.15 Hz) fluctuations that are synchronized across different regions of the brain.
source: The BOLD signal exhibits low frequency (~0.01–0.15 Hz) fluctuations that are synchronized across different regions of the brain, a phenomenon known as functional connectivity (FC).
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about BOLD signal characteristics.

claim: Functional connectivity (FC) has been observed even in the absence of any explicit stimulus or task, giving rise to resting-state networks (RSNs).
source: FC has been observed even in the absence of any explicit stimulus or task, giving rise to the so-called resting-state networks (RSNs) (Biswal et al., 1995; Fox and Raichle, 2007; Smith et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational studies on resting-state networks.

claim: FC was initially viewed as a stationary phenomenon (static FC) and was commonly measured as the correlation between brain regions over an entire scan.
source: Initially, FC was viewed as a stationary phenomenon (static FC) and was commonly measured as the correlation between brain regions over an entire scan.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the historical approach to FC analysis.

claim: Several researchers challenged the assumption that FC is stationary.
source: However, several researchers challenged this assumption (Chang and Glover, 2010; Sakoğlu et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that challenged the stationarity assumption.

claim: Recent studies have been focusing on FC dynamics, quantified over shorter time scales than the scan duration (time-varying FC).
source: recent studies have been focusing on FC dynamics, quantified over shorter time scales than the scan duration (time-varying FC) (Hutchison et al., 2013; Lurie et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent review studies on time-varying FC.

claim: In animal models, a strong association between spontaneous BOLD fluctuations and neural activity, in particular band-limited local field potentials and firing rates, has been reported.
source: For instance, in animal models, a strong association between spontaneous BOLD fluctuations and neural activity, in particular band-limited local field potentials and firing rates, has been reported (Logothetis et al., 2001; Schölvinck et al., 2010; Shmuel and Leopold, 2008; Thompson et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal studies demonstrating the neural basis of BOLD fluctuations.

claim: A recent study suggested a close correspondence between windowed FC calculated from simultaneously recorded hemodynamic signals and calcium transients.
source: Furthermore, a recent study suggested a close correspondence between windowed FC calculated from simultaneously recorded hemodynamic signals and calcium transients (Matsui et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study using calcium imaging.

claim: In human studies, direct measurements of macroscale neural activity have revealed a spatial correlation structure similar to that of spontaneous BOLD fluctuations.
source: In human studies, direct measurements of macroscale neural activity have revealed a spatial correlation structure similar to that of spontaneous BOLD fluctuations (Brookes et al., 2011; Hacker et al., 2017; He et al., 2008; Hipp et al., 2012; Kucyi et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human studies using direct neural measurements.

claim: At least 50% of the spontaneous hemodynamic signal is unrelated to ongoing neural activity.
source: However, BOLD signals rely on changes in local cerebral blood flow (CBF) to infer underlying changes in neuronal activity, and according to a recent study, at least 50% of the spontaneous hemodynamic signal is unrelated to ongoing neural activity (Winder et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study quantifying the non-neural component of hemodynamic signals.

claim: Low frequency variations in breathing activity account for a considerable fraction of variance of the BOLD signal.
source: In particular, low frequency variations in breathing activity (Birn et al., 2008b; Birn et al., 2006; Power et al., 2017), arterial blood pressure (Whittaker et al., 2019), arterial CO2 concentration (Prokopiou et al., 2019; Wise et al., 2004), and heart rate (Chang et al., 2009; Shmueli et al., 2007) are known to account for a considerable fraction of variance of the BOLD signal, presumably through changes in CBF.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating the effect of breathing on BOLD signals.

claim: Low frequency variations in arterial blood pressure account for a considerable fraction of variance of the BOLD signal.
source: In particular, low frequency variations in breathing activity (Birn et al., 2008b; Birn et al., 2006; Power et al., 2017), arterial blood pressure (Whittaker et al., 2019), arterial CO2 concentration (Prokopiou et al., 2019; Wise et al., 2004), and heart rate (Chang et al., 2009; Shmueli et al., 2007) are known to account for a considerable fraction of variance of the BOLD signal, presumably through changes in CBF.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on blood pressure effects.

claim: Low frequency variations in arterial CO2 concentration account for a considerable fraction of variance of the BOLD signal.
source: In particular, low frequency variations in breathing activity (Birn et al., 2008b; Birn et al., 2006; Power et al., 2017), arterial blood pressure (Whittaker et al., 2019), arterial CO2 concentration (Prokopiou et al., 2019; Wise et al., 2004), and heart rate (Chang et al., 2009; Shmueli et al., 2007) are known to account for a considerable fraction of variance of the BOLD signal, presumably through changes in CBF.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on CO2 effects.

claim: Low frequency variations in heart rate account for a considerable fraction of variance of the BOLD signal.
source: In particular, low frequency variations in breathing activity (Birn et al., 2008b; Birn et al., 2006; Power et al., 2017), arterial blood pressure (Whittaker et al., 2019), arterial CO2 concentration (Prokopiou et al., 2019; Wise et al., 2004), and heart rate (Chang et al., 2009; Shmueli et al., 2007) are known to account for a considerable fraction of variance of the BOLD signal, presumably through changes in CBF.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on heart rate effects.

claim: The BOLD signal intensity is distorted by high-frequency physiological fluctuations, such as cardiovascular pulsation and breathing, through displacement of the brain tissues and perturbations of the B0 magnetic field.
source: In addition, the BOLD signal intensity is distorted by high-frequency physiological fluctuations, such as cardiovascular pulsation and breathing, through displacement of the brain tissues and perturbations of the B0 magnetic field (Dagli et al., 1999; Glover et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on high-frequency physiological artifacts.

claim: Head motion has a substantial impact on fMRI through partial volume, magnetic inhomogeneity and spin-history effects.
source: Further, head motion is well-known to have a substantial impact on fMRI through partial volume, magnetic inhomogeneity and spin-history effects (Friston et al., 1996; Power et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational studies on motion artifacts.

claim: Non-neuronal factors may introduce common variance components in signals recorded from different brain regions and subsequently induce spurious correlations between these areas.
source: These non-neuronal factors may introduce common variance components in signals recorded from different brain regions and subsequently induce spurious correlations between these areas (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating spurious correlations from physiological confounds.

claim: Static and time-varying resting-state FC have shown promise for providing concise descriptions of how the brain changes across the lifespan.
source: Static and time-varying resting-state FC have shown promise for providing concise descriptions of how the brain changes across the lifespan (Battaglia et al., 2020; Chan et al., 2014; Ferreira et al., 2016; Geerligs et al., 2015; Sala-Llonch et al., 2015; Xia et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on lifespan changes in FC.

claim: Static and time-varying resting-state FC have shown promise to assay neural differences that are associated with disease.
source: and to assay neural differences that are associated with disease (Baker et al., 2014b; Chen et al., 2017; Damaraju et al., 2014; Demirtaş et al., 2016; Drysdale et al., 2017; Du et al., 2016; Gratton et al., 2019; Hahamy et al., 2015; Mash et al., 2019; Morgan et al., 2017; Xia et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on disease-related FC differences.

claim: There is always a trade-off between adequately removing confounds from fMRI data and preserving the signal of interest.
source: However, recent studies assessing the performance of a large range of preprocessing strategies found that there is always a trade-off between adequately removing confounds from fMRI data and preserving the signal of interest (Ciric et al., 2017; Kassinopoulos and Mitsis, 2021a; Parkes et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies evaluating preprocessing strategies.

claim: Widely used techniques for the preprocessing of fMRI data may not efficiently remove physiological and motion artifacts.
source: Importantly, these studies found that widely used techniques for the preprocessing of fMRI data may not efficiently remove physiological and motion artifacts.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cited preprocessing studies.

claim: Vascular responses following systemic changes are spatially heterogenous.
source: Several studies have examined whether physiological fluctuations across the brain could give rise to structured spatial patterns that resemble common RSNs, based on the evidence that vascular responses following systemic changes are spatially heterogenous (Chang et al., 2009; Pinto et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on spatial heterogeneity of vascular responses.

claim: Bright and Murphy, 2015 applied independent component analysis (ICA) to the fraction of the fMRI data explained by nuisance regressors related to head motion and physiological variability and revealed a characteristic network structure similar to previously reported RSNs.
source: For instance, Bright and Murphy, 2015 applied independent component analysis (ICA) to the fraction of the fMRI data explained by nuisance regressors related to head motion and physiological variability and revealed a characteristic network structure similar to previously reported RSNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Tong et al., 2013; Tong and Frederick, 2014 found significant contributions of systemic fluctuations on ICA time courses related to the visual, sensorimotor and auditory networks.
source: Similarly, Tong et al., 2013; Tong and Frederick, 2014 found significant contributions of systemic fluctuations on ICA time courses related to the visual, sensorimotor and auditory networks.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Chen et al., 2020 generated BOLD data containing only slow respiratory-related dynamics and showed that respiratory variation can give rise to apparent neurally-related connectivity patterns.
source: Recently, Chen et al., 2020 generated BOLD data containing only slow respiratory-related dynamics and showed that respiratory variation can give rise to apparent neurally-related connectivity patterns.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Physiological confounds can modulate time-varying FC measures.
source: Further, recent investigations have shown that physiological confounds can modulate time-varying FC measures (Chang et al., 2013; Nalci et al., 2019; Nikolaou et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on time-varying FC confounds.

claim: Cardiac autonomic dysregulation has been associated to a variety of psychiatric disorders.
source: For instance, cardiac autonomic dysregulation has been associated to a variety of psychiatric disorders (Alvares et al., 2016; Benjamin et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on cardiac dysregulation in psychiatric disorders.

claim: Connectivity profiles vary substantially between individuals, acting as an identifying fingerprint.
source: Recent studies have shown that connectivity profiles vary substantially between individuals, acting as an identifying fingerprint (Finn et al., 2015; Miranda-Dominguez et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to fingerprinting studies.

claim: Connectivity fingerprints are stable over long periods of time.
source: that is stable over long periods of time (Horien et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a longitudinal study.

claim: The high subject discriminability of connectivity profiles may arise partly as a result of physiological processes being highly subject-specific.
source: However, the high subject discriminability of connectivity profiles may arise partly as a result of physiological processes (Batchvarov et al., 2002; Golestani et al., 2015; Malik et al., 2008; Pinna et al., 2007; Pitzalis et al., 1996; Power et al., 2020; Reland et al., 2005) and head motion (Van Dijk et al., 2012; Zeng et al., 2014) being highly subject-specific.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on subject-specific physiological and motion characteristics.

claim: The mean of intraclass correlation values of functional connections is reduced when a relatively aggressive pipeline is used.
source: Evidence supporting this hypothesis comes from studies showing that the mean of intraclass correlation values of functional connections, associated to test-retest reliability across sessions, is reduced when a relatively aggressive pipeline is used (Birn et al., 2014; Kassinopoulos and Mitsis, 2021a; Parkes et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to preprocessing studies.

claim: Artifacts exhibit high subject specificity.
source: suggesting that artifacts exhibit high subject specificity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that aggressive preprocessing reduces test-retest reliability.

claim: SLFOs mostly affected sensory regions, including the visual and somatosensory cortices (particularly of the face).
source: The results showed distinct regional patterns for each of the nuisance processes. SLFOs mostly affected sensory regions, including the visual and somatosensory cortices (particularly of the face) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Phase encoding was not found to modulate the magnitude of the SLFOs contributions on the BOLD signal.
source: Phase encoding was not found to modulate the magnitude of the SLFOs contributions on the BOLD signal (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Head motion exhibited the largest effect in the somatosensory and visual cortices.
source: Head motion exhibited the largest effect in the somatosensory and visual cortices (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The effect of head motion in the visual cortex was highest in the right hemisphere for LR phase encoding, but highest in the left hemisphere for RL phase encoding.
source: Intriguingly, the effect in the visual cortex was highest in the right hemisphere for LR phase encoding, but highest in the left hemisphere for RL phase encoding (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Breathing motion effects were more pronounced in prefrontal, parietal and temporal brain regions.
source: Breathing motion effects were more pronounced in prefrontal, parietal and temporal brain regions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Breathing motion had a much larger impact on the left hemisphere when the phase encoding was LR, whereas the reverse pattern was observed for RL phase encoding.
source: Further, breathing motion had a much larger impact on the left hemisphere when the phase encoding was LR, whereas the reverse pattern was observed for RL phase encoding (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cardiac pulsatility was highest in regions such as the visual and auditory cortices, as well as the insular cortex.
source: Cardiac pulsatility was highest in regions such as the visual and auditory cortices, as well as the insular cortex (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The group-averaged static FC matrices across all 1568 scans revealed consistent whole-brain connectome patterns for SLFOs, head motion and breathing motion.
source: The group-averaged static FC matrices across all 1568 scans revealed consistent whole-brain connectome patterns for SLFOs, head motion and breathing motion (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: SLFO-based connectivity profiles exhibited strong positive correlations for all edges of the FC matrix, particularly for edges within the visual network, as well as between the visual network and the rest of the brain.
source: SLFO-based connectivity profiles exhibited strong positive correlations for all edges of the FC matrix, particularly for edges within the visual network, as well as between the visual network and the rest of the brain (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Head motion mainly influenced functional connections within the visual and sensorimotor networks, as well as edges within the DMN.
source: Head motion mainly influenced functional connections within the visual and sensorimotor networks, as well as edges within the DMN (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Breathing motion exhibited an intriguing chess-like pattern, with both positive and negative correlations.
source: Breathing motion exhibited an intriguing chess-like pattern, with both positive and negative correlations (Figure 2C, lower triangular matrix).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: For breathing motion, positive correlations were mostly confined between ROIs of the same hemisphere, whereas correlations between hemispheres were close to zero or even negative.
source: Based on this observation, we subsequently reordered the ROIs with respect to their hemisphere, which revealed that positive correlations were mostly confined between ROIs of the same hemisphere, whereas correlations between hemispheres were close to zero or even negative (Figure 2C, upper triangular matrix).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Cardiac pulsatility did not exhibit a characteristic spatial pattern and the group-averaged correlation values were low, suggesting that it does not affect static FC in a systematic manner across subjects.
source: Finally, cardiac pulsatility did not exhibit a characteristic spatial pattern and the group-averaged correlation values were low, suggesting that it does not affect static FC in a systematic manner across subjects (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and inference from the observed pattern.

claim: SLFOs, head motion and breathing motion were found to confound the FC matrices more severely than cardiac pulsatility.
source: We found that SLFOs, head motion and breathing motion had the strongest influence on static FC, based on the similarity of their connectome profiles with the 'neural' connectome profiles from the raw data (Figure 2E–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E-H.

claim: The signature induced by SLFOs remained after the MildA, MildB, and FIX pipelines were applied, but was greatly reduced by the WM50 and WM200 strategies.
source: The signature induced by SLFOs remained after the MildA, MildB, and FIX pipelines were applied, but was greatly reduced by the WM50 and WM200 strategies (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: FIX is unable to remove most of the SLFOs.
source: The observation that FIX, which is a rather aggressive preprocessing strategy, was unable to remove most of the SLFOs is consistent with recent studies showing that global artifactual fluctuations are still prominent after FIX denoising (Burgess et al., 2016; Glasser et al., 2018; Kassinopoulos and Mitsis, 2019; Power et al., 2018; Power et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2E and citations to studies on FIX limitations.

claim: GSR is an effective technique for removing the physiological signature from SLFOs on static FC.
source: Notably, GSR seemed to be an effective technique for removing the physiological signature from SLFOs on static FC, albeit for some scans it appeared to introduce a negative correlation between the SLFOs and 'neural' FC matrices (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The effect of the signature related to head motion was reduced with more aggressive preprocessing strategies, but none of the examined approaches completely eradicated the head motion effects in static FC.
source: The effect of the signature related to head motion was reduced with more aggressive preprocessing strategies, but none of the examined approaches completely eradicated the head motion effects in static FC (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The signature induced by breathing motion was greatly reduced by all preprocessing strategies, and particularly by FIX denoising.
source: The signature induced by breathing motion was greatly reduced by all preprocessing strategies, and particularly by FIX denoising, which yielded almost chance level (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The confounds introduced by cardiac pulsatility were overall small and effectively removed by the FIX, WM50, and WM200 strategies.
source: The confounds introduced by cardiac pulsatility were overall small and effectively removed by the FIX, WM50, and WM200 strategies (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Including the regressor that models SLFOs reduces their effect on static FC for all preprocessing strategies apart from WM50 and WM200.
source: We found that including the regressor that models SLFOs reduces their effect on static FC for all preprocessing strategies apart from WM50 and WM200, but, in contrast to GSR, the similarity remains well above chance levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Including the RETROICOR regressors related to cardiac pulsatility completely removed the effect of the latter for the raw data and the MildA and MildB strategies.
source: On the contrary, including the RETROICOR regressors related to cardiac pulsatility completely removed the effect of the latter for the raw data and the MildA and MildB strategies (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Accuracy was above chance for all database-target combinations for the nuisance processes, with rates up to 40%.
source: Accuracy was above chance for all database-target combinations for the nuisance processes, with rates up to 40% (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For breathing motion, database-target pairs that had the same phase encoding yielded much higher identification rates than database-target pairs with different phase encodings.
source: Breathing motion exhibited an intriguing bimodal distribution: database-target pairs that had the same phase encoding yielded much higher identification rates than database-target pairs with different phase encodings, even if the latter were acquired on the same day.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Identification accuracy was much higher for the 'neural' datasets compared to the nuisance datasets, with rates ranging from 52% to 99%.
source: Identification accuracy was much higher for the 'neural' datasets compared to the nuisance datasets, with rates ranging from 52% to 99% (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The WM50 and WM200 techniques significantly outperformed all other preprocessing strategies in terms of identification accuracy.
source: The MildA, MildB, and FIX techniques considerably improved the accuracy compared to the raw data, and the WM50 and WM200 techniques significantly outperformed all other preprocessing strategies.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: GSR considerably improved identification accuracy for the MildA, MildB and FIX strategies.
source: GSR considerably improved identification accuracy for the MildA, MildB and FIX strategies.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Functional connections between networks contributed more to the subject discriminability of SLFOs compared to connections within brain networks.
source: Furthermore, functional connections between networks seemed to contribute more to the subject discriminability of SLFOs compared to connections within brain networks (p<0.001, Wilcoxon rank-sum).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical testing of data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Networks of 'top-down' control (FPN, CO, DAN, VAN), as well as the DMN, yielded higher identification accuracy compared to sensorimotor processing networks (Visual, SMd, Aud) for all preprocessing strategies.
source: Networks of 'top-down' control (FPN, CO, DAN, VAN), as well as the DMN, yielded higher identification accuracy compared to sensorimotor processing networks (Visual, SMd, Aud) for all preprocessing strategies (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: FC patterns in higher order association cortices ('top-down' control networks) tend to be distinctive for each individual, whereas primary sensory and motor regions (processing networks) tend to exhibit similar patterns across individuals.
source: These results indicate that FC patterns in higher order association cortices ('top-down' control networks) tend to be distinctive for each individual, whereas primary sensory and motor regions (processing networks) tend to exhibit similar patterns across individuals, consistent with previous studies (Finn et al., 2015; Gratton et al., 2018; Horien et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: WM200 denoising significantly increased the subject discriminability of connections within and between all top-down control networks, connections within the Visual and SMd networks, and connections of the DAN with the Visual and SMd network.
source: Conversely, WM200 denoising significantly increased the subject discriminability of connections within and between all top-down control networks, connections within the Visual and SMd networks, and connections of the DAN with the Visual and SMd network.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical testing of data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The temporal evolution of FC patterns from SLFOs and head motion were similar to the ones observed in the raw data.
source: We observed that the temporal evolution of FC patterns from SLFOs and head motion were similar to the ones observed in the raw data.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 6.

claim: The distribution of similarity values for breathing motion and cardiac pulsatility FCD matrices was around zero, indicating the absence of systematic effects on 'neural' FCD matrices.
source: On the other hand, the distribution of similarity values for breathing motion and cardiac pulsatility FCD matrices was around zero, indicating the absence of systematic effects on 'neural' FCD matrices (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: None of the preprocessing pipelines was able to vanish the effects of SLFOs and head motion on time-varying FC.
source: None of the preprocessing pipelines was able to vanish the effects of SLFOs and head motion.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 6.

claim: The effects of SLFOs and head motion on time-varying FC were considerably reduced by the WM50 and WM200 strategies.
source: However, these effects were considerably reduced by the WM50 and WM200 strategies (Figure 5A–B, Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A-B and Figure 6.

claim: FIX denoising was the least successful strategy in terms of reducing the SLFOs' signature on time-varying FC.
source: FIX denoising was the least successful strategy in terms of reducing the SLFOs' signature (Figure 5A, Figure 6), similarly to static FC (Figure 2E)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 6.

claim: SLFOs related to changes in heart rate and breathing patterns were found to affect mostly sensory regions including the visual and somatosensory cortices, which correspond to regions with a high density of veins.
source: SLFOs related to changes in heart rate and breathing patterns were found to affect mostly sensory regions including the visual and somatosensory cortices (particularly of the face) (Figure 1A), which correspond to regions with a high density of veins (Bernier et al., 2018; Huck et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1A and citations to studies on venous density.

claim: The spatial pattern of SLFOs is very similar to statistical maps reported in prior works, which have highlighted brain regions highly correlated with the global signal.
source: The spatial pattern of SLFOs is very similar to statistical maps reported in prior works, which have highlighted brain regions highly correlated with the global signal (Billings and Keilholz, 2018; Glasser et al., 2016; Li et al., 2019a; Power et al., 2017; Tong et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The global signal is strongly driven by fluctuations in heart rate and breathing patterns.
source: This is not surprising, since the global signal is strongly driven by fluctuations in heart rate and breathing patterns (Birn et al., 2006; Chang and Glover, 2009a; Falahpour et al., 2013; Kassinopoulos and Mitsis, 2019; Shmueli et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on the global signal.

claim: SLFOs and cardiac pulsatility do not affect the same brain regions.
source: Moreover, we show evidence that SLFOs and cardiac pulsatility do not affect the same brain regions, consistent with (Chen et al., 2019; Kassinopoulos and Mitsis, 2019; Tong and Frederick, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1 and citations to previous studies.

claim: Cardiac pulsatility was more dominant in regions such as the insular and auditory cortices, which align with cortical branches of the middle cerebral artery and are the regions with highest arterial density.
source: Specifically, cardiac pulsatility was more dominant in regions such as the insular and auditory cortices, which align with cortical branches of the middle cerebral artery (Figure 1D) and are the regions with highest arterial density (Bernier et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1D and a citation to a study on arterial density.

claim: Sensorimotor and visual areas were strongly affected by head motion.
source: In the present work, we regressed out breathing motion from the realignment parameters, and observed that sensorimotor and visual areas were strongly affected by head motion (Figure 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Breathing motion artifacts were more pronounced in the prefrontal cortex and brain regions in the parietal and temporal cortices.
source: whereas breathing motion artifacts were more pronounced in the prefrontal cortex and brain regions in the parietal and temporal cortices (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The structure of the SLFOs' connectome profile may largely reflect the underlying vascular architecture.
source: Therefore, it is likely that the structure of the SLFOs' connectome profile may largely reflect the underlying vascular architecture.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed patterns and known vascular density.

claim: Head motion was found to influence the connectivity within the visual and sensorimotor networks.
source: Head motion was found to influence the connectivity within the visual and sensorimotor networks (Figure 2B), in line with previous studies (Power et al., 2012; Satterthwaite et al., 2012; Van Dijk et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2B and citations to previous studies.

claim: Only regressing out the realignment parameters and average WM/CSF signals (with or without expansion terms) is not sufficient to remove the effects of head motion.
source: Our results showed that only regressing out the realignment parameters and average WM/CSF signals (with or without expansion terms) is not sufficient to remove the effects of head motion (Figure 2F, MildA and MildB pipelines), which is consistent with findings in Parkes et al., 2018.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2F and a citation to a previous study.

claim: Among all preprocessing strategies, WM denoising yielded the largest reduction of motion effects.
source: Among all preprocessing strategies, WM denoising yielded the largest reduction of motion effects (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The more aggressive WM200 resulted in a larger reduction of motion artifacts compared to WM50.
source: In our previous study, we showed that while both pipelines yielded high large-scale network identifiability compared to other pipelines, the more aggressive WM200 resulted in a larger reduction of motion artifacts compared to WM50 (Kassinopoulos and Mitsis, 2021a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Head and breathing motion do not affect functional connectivity in the same manner.
source: Furthermore, we provide evidence that head and breathing motion do not affect functional connectivity in the same manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Breathing motion was found to inflate within-hemisphere connectivity.
source: Specifically, breathing motion was found to inflate within-hemisphere connectivity (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The bias from breathing motion seems to arise as a result of factitious motion rather than real motion of the head, since it is related to the LR/RL phase encoding direction.
source: This bias seems to arise as a result of factitious motion rather than real motion of the head, since it is related to the LR/RL phase encoding direction (see section 4.4 for more details).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed phase encoding dependence.

claim: All preprocessing strategies yielded a substantial reduction of artifacts related to breathing motion, with FIX denoising being the most effective.
source: All preprocessing strategies yielded a substantial reduction of artifacts related to breathing motion, with FIX denoising being the most effective (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The 3T HCP dataset has poor temporal signal-to-noise ratio in the subcortex.
source: However, it has been recently reported that the 3T HCP dataset has poor temporal signal-to-noise ratio in the subcortex (Ji et al., 2019; Seitzman et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on HCP data quality.

claim: It is possible that the effect of cardiac pulsatility in functional connections involving subcortical regions may have been underestimated.
source: Therefore, it is possible that we may have underestimated the effect of cardiac pulsatility in functional connections involving subcortical regions.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the known limitations of the dataset.

claim: Physiological fluctuations give rise to networks that spatially resemble neurally driven networks linked to working memory and visual stimuli.
source: A recent study by Bright et al., 2020 provided evidence that physiological fluctuations (end-tidal CO2) give rise to networks that spatially resemble neurally driven networks linked to working memory and visual stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Vascular and neuronal growth processes evolve concurrently during development.
source: The authors suggested that this phenomenon may be due to the vasculature adapting to the neural network architecture, as vascular and neuronal growth processes evolve concurrently during development (Quaegebeur et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on neurovascular development.

claim: FIX and WM denoising combined with GSR demonstrate the highest improvement in large-scale network identifiability.
source: Nonetheless, the pre-processing strategies that were found in this study to reduce the nuisance effects the most (i.e. FIX and WM denoising combined with GSR) have been shown to demonstrate the highest improvement in large-scale network identifiability in an earlier study (Kassinopoulos and Mitsis, 2021a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: FIX and WM denoising combined with GSR are able to adequately remove the effects of nuisance processes while also preserving the signal of interest.
source: These results suggest that they are able to adequately remove the effects of nuisance processes while also preserving the signal of interest.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed high network identifiability and fingerprinting accuracy.

claim: Variations in FC over shorter time-scales (i.e. minutes) could largely be explained by sampling error, acquisition artifacts and subject arousal.
source: For instance, variations in FC over shorter time-scales (i.e. minutes) could largely be explained by sampling error, acquisition artifacts and subject arousal (Hindriks et al., 2016; Laumann et al., 2017; Savva et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on time-varying FC confounds.

claim: Even after regressing out nuisance processes from the BOLD signal, correlations between time-varying FC measures and nuisance fluctuations remain.
source: These results are aligned with the observation that even after regressing out nuisance processes from the BOLD signal, correlations between time-varying FC measures and nuisance fluctuations remain (Nalci et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A significant fraction of the variability in FC patterns is a result of non-neural confounds and WM denoising is able to remove most of these confounds.
source: These results can be interpreted in two ways that are not mutually exclusive: (1) A significant fraction of the variability in FC patterns is a result of non-neural confounds and WM denoising is able to remove most of these confounds.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on interpretation of the observed results.

claim: WM denoising removes a considerable fraction of variance of neural origin.
source: (2) WM denoising removes a considerable fraction of variance of neural origin.
evidence: This claim is speculative, representing an alternative interpretation of the results.

claim: The effects of breathing motion and cardiac pulsatility do not influence time-varying FC, because their effect on the BOLD signal does not change from window to window, possibly due to their quasi-periodic nature.
source: Likely, the effects of breathing motion and cardiac pulsatility do not influence time-varying FC, because their effect on the BOLD signal does not change from window to window, possibly due to their quasi-periodic nature.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed lack of effect.

claim: ROIs sensitive to head motion and SLFOs are likely to exhibit a time-varying signal-to-noise ratio depending on the presence of these sources of noise, which eventually leads to confounds in time-varying FC measures.
source: In other words, ROIs sensitive to head motion and SLFOs are likely to exhibit a time-varying signal-to-noise ratio depending on the presence of these sources of noise, which eventually leads to confounds in time-varying FC measures.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed effects on time-varying FC.

claim: GSR removes physiological fluctuations related to SLFOs and to a lesser extent head motion artifacts.
source: Our results provide evidence that, in the context of static FC, GSR removes physiological fluctuations related to SLFOs and to a lesser extent head motion artifacts (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: GSR improved connectome fingerprinting accuracy.
source: Furthermore, GSR improved connectome fingerprinting accuracy (Figure 3B)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: By removing nuisance fluctuations due to SLFOs and head motion, GSR enhances the individual specificity of connectivity profiles.
source: which suggests that by removing nuisance fluctuations due to SLFOs and head motion, GSR enhances the individual specificity of connectivity profiles.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed improvement in fingerprinting accuracy.

claim: The strong reduction in the effects of SLFOs and head motion achieved by GSR outweighs the possible loss of neuronal-driven fluctuations when examining FC patterns.
source: Overall, our results suggest that the strong reduction in the effects of SLFOs and head motion achieved by GSR outweighs the possible loss of neuronal-driven fluctuations when examining FC patterns.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the overall results on GSR effectiveness.

claim: GSR is particularly important when using ICA-based noise correction techniques such as FIX and AROMA, since ICA components related to SLFOs frequently exhibit similar spatial patterns and frequency profile to neural components and thus are classified as non-artifactual and remain in the data after denoising.
source: GSR is particularly important when using ICA-based noise correction techniques such as FIX and AROMA (Pruim et al., 2015; Salimi-Khorshidi et al., 2014), since ICA components related to SLFOs frequently exhibit similar spatial patterns and frequency profile to neural components and thus are classified as non-artifactual and remain in the data after denoising.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed limitations of ICA-based methods and citations to these methods.

claim: Scans that exhibited a negative SLFOs-neural similarity after GSR were scans where a large fraction of the GS variance was attributed to SLFOs.
source: Further investigation revealed that scans that exhibited a negative SLFOs-neural similarity after GSR were scans where a large fraction of the GS variance was attributed to SLFOs (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The use of a single global regressor for the estimation of the SLFOs signature does not account for variability in the dynamics of SLFOs across brain regions.
source: A possible explanation for the low contribution of SLFOs in the somatosensory and auditory networks is the use of a single global regressor for the estimation of the SLFOs signature, which does not account for variability in the dynamics of SLFOs across brain regions.
evidence: This claim is speculative, representing a possible explanation for the observed pattern.

claim: Primary sensory areas exhibit a different respiration response function (RRF) compared to other areas.
source: Interestingly, the primary sensory areas that belong to the two aforementioned networks were also reported in the work by Chen et al., 2020 as exhibiting a different respiration response function (RRF) compared to other areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Modeling SLFOs at the individual level could potentially be improved if spatial variability in RRF is also accounted for.
source: These findings suggest that modeling SLFOs at the individual level could potentially be improved if spatial variability in RRF is also accounted for.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed spatial variability.

claim: The effects of SLFOs cannot be corrected equally well in all areas solely by regressing out the GS.
source: Moreover, these results indicate that the effects of SLFOs cannot be corrected equally well in all areas solely by regressing out the GS.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed regional differences in GSR effectiveness.

claim: The negative SLFOs-neural similarity was substantially decreased when GSR is combined with white matter denoising.
source: Related to this, we also observed that the negative SLFOs-neural similarity was substantially decreased when GSR is combined with white matter denoising
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis.

claim: Nuisance regressors obtained from white matter can reduce fluctuations induced by SLFOs in all areas, including primary sensory areas, better than GSR alone.
source: which may suggest that the nuisance regressors obtained from white matter can reduce fluctuations induced by SLFOs in all areas, including primary sensory areas, better than GSR alone.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed improvement when combining GSR with WM denoising.

claim: Incorporating GSR in the preprocessing improved the identification of modularity in functional networks in time-varying FC.
source: Nonetheless, a recent study evaluating preprocessing strategies in the context of time-varying FC showed that incorporating GSR in the preprocessing improved the identification of modularity in functional networks (Lydon-Staley et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: GSR was able to remove nuisance processes related to scanner instabilities, CO2 concentration and finger skin vascular tone.
source: This may indicate that GSR was able to remove nuisance processes that we did not evaluate in the current study. These processes may be related to scanner instabilities, CO2 concentration (Power et al., 2017; Wise et al., 2004) and finger skin vascular tone (Kassinopoulos and Mitsis, 2021b; Özbay et al., 2019), which are known to be reflected on the GS.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference and citations to studies on other nuisance processes.

claim: Chest wall movements due to breathing perturb the B0 field.
source: Earlier studies have demonstrated that chest wall movements due to breathing perturb the B0 field (Raj et al., 2001; Raj et al., 2000; Van de Moortele et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Breathing causes factitious motion of the fMRI volumes in the phase encoding direction.
source: (1) Breathing causes factitious motion of the fMRI volumes in the phase encoding direction (Raj et al., 2001; Raj et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Breathing induces artifacts on voxel timeseries that depend on the location of those voxels along the phase encoding direction.
source: (2) Breathing induces artifacts on voxel timeseries that depend on the location of those voxels along the phase encoding direction (Raj et al., 2001; Raj et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Depending on the phase encoding direction (LR or RL), breathing motion artifacts were more pronounced in the left or right hemisphere respectively.
source: Specifically, we found that depending on the phase encoding direction (LR or RL), breathing motion artifacts were more pronounced in the left or right hemisphere respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Breathing motion increased within-hemisphere connectivity for both phase encoding scan types.
source: Moreover, we observed that breathing motion increased within-hemisphere connectivity for both phase encoding scan types (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Breathing induces artifactual fluctuations that are to a certain extent different between hemispheres.
source: which implies that breathing induces artifactual fluctuations that are to a certain extent different between hemispheres.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed within-hemisphere connectivity increase.

claim: Factitious rather than real motion is the predominant source of respiration-related motion artifacts in fMRI.
source: Thus, studies that consider datasets with different phase encodings, should be aware of the effect of phase encoding on FC, especially if data from different groups have been acquired with different phase encodings.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the phase encoding dependence and supported by a citation.

claim: Nuisance processes can have an impact on test-retest reliability, given the subject-specific nature of physiological processes and head motion.
source: However, apart from neural processes, nuisance processes can also have an impact on test-retest reliability, given the subject-specific nature of physiological processes (Batchvarov et al., 2002; Golestani et al., 2015; Malik et al., 2008; Pinna et al., 2007; Pitzalis et al., 1996; Power et al., 2020; Reland et al., 2005) and head motion (Van Dijk et al., 2012; Zeng et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on subject-specific characteristics.

claim: The median of intraclass correlation values across functional connections is reduced when a relatively aggressive pipeline is used.
source: For instance, it has been reported that the median of intraclass correlation values across functional connections, which is a metric of test-retest reliability, is reduced when a relatively aggressive pipeline is used (Birn et al., 2014; Parkes et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to preprocessing studies.

claim: Motion can classify subjects at above-chance levels.
source: Furthermore, motion can classify subjects at above-chance levels (Horien et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Breathing motion is more prominent in older individuals and those with a higher body mass index.
source: and breathing motion is more prominent in older individuals and those with a higher body mass index (Gratton et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: All nuisance processes exhibited identification accuracy above chance level.
source: All nuisance processes exhibited identification accuracy above chance level (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There is some degree of subject discriminability in nuisance processes.
source: Overall, our results suggest that there is some degree of subject discriminability in nuisance processes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the above-chance identification accuracy of nuisance processes.

claim: The high subject discriminability of SLFOs suggests a certain degree of idiosyncrasy that is possibly related to the vascular architecture of an individual.
source: Given the nature of SLFOs (i.e. they affect the BOLD signal through changes in CBF), the high subject discriminability of SLFOs suggests a certain degree of idiosyncrasy that is possibly related to the vascular architecture of an individual.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed subject discriminability.

claim: The high subject discriminability observed in the HCP data is not due to the presence of confounds.
source: WM denoising, which was found to be the most effective strategy for reducing confounds due to head motion and physiological fluctuations (Figure 2E–H), yielded also the highest accuracy in connectome fingerprinting (Figure 3B), suggesting that the high subject discriminability observed in the HCP data is not due to the presence of confounds.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that better denoising improves fingerprinting accuracy.

claim: The functional connectome of a subject reflects some aspects of their vigilance levels.
source: Possible explanations for this finding are that the functional connectome of a subject reflects some aspects of their vigilance levels (Tagliazucchi and Laufs, 2014; Thompson et al., 2013a; Wang et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is speculative, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The functional connectome of a subject reflects mind-wandering.
source: mind-wandering (Gonzalez-Castillo et al., 2019; Gorgolewski et al., 2014; Kucyi, 2018; Kucyi and Davis, 2014)
evidence: This claim is speculative, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The functional connectome of a subject reflects the effect of time of day.
source: or the effect of time of day (Hodkinson et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2016; Orban et al., 2020; Shannon et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is speculative, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The high connectome-based identification accuracies reported in the literature do not appear to be driven by nuisance confounds, suggesting a neural origin underpinning the inter-individual differences in connectivity.
source: Overall, the high connectome-based identification accuracies reported in the literature do not appear to be driven by nuisance confounds, suggesting a neural origin underpinning the inter-individual differences in connectivity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the overall fingerprinting results.

claim: Subject variability in the magnitude of functional connections arises as a result of spatial topographical variability in the location of functional regions across individuals.
source: Nonetheless, it is worth pointing out that subject variability in the magnitude of functional connections has been shown to arise as a result of spatial topographical variability in the location of functional regions across individuals (Bijsterbosch et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Association cortices are the most evolutionarily recent.
source: The fact that association cortices are the most evolutionarily recent (Zilles et al., 1988)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Association cortices are thought to be involved in higher level functions.
source: and are thought to be involved in higher level functions (Cole et al., 2014; Cole et al., 2013; Dosenbach et al., 2007; Gratton et al., 2017; Raichle, 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Medial frontal and frontoparietal networks exhibit the highest identification accuracy as a result of being less prone to distortions from susceptibility artifacts.
source: On the other hand, it has also been speculated that medial frontal and frontoparietal networks exhibit the highest identification accuracy as a result of being less prone to distortions from susceptibility artifacts (Horien et al., 2019; Noble et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is speculative, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The basis of the high identification rates for association cortices is of neural origin.
source: These results seem to indicate that the basis of the high identification rates for association cortices is of neural origin
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that preprocessing does not reduce identification accuracy for these networks.

claim: Resting-state fMRI-based connectome fingerprinting can capture idiosyncratic aspects of cognition reflected on the resting-state functional characteristics of the association cortex.
source: and thus that resting-state fMRI-based connectome fingerprinting can capture idiosyncratic aspects of cognition reflected on the resting-state functional characteristics of the association cortex.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the high identification accuracy of association cortices.

claim: Head motion and systemic BOLD fluctuations associated to changes in heart rate and breathing patterns cause systematic biases in static FC and result in recurrent patterns in time-varying FC.
source: Our results suggest that head motion and systemic BOLD fluctuations associated to changes in heart rate and breathing patterns cause systematic biases in static FC and result in recurrent patterns in time-varying FC.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the overall results of the study.

claim: Data-driven techniques based on decomposing the data into principal or independent components (PCA, ICA), combined with GSR, lead to the strongest reduction of head motion and SLFO effects.
source: Data-driven techniques based on decomposing the data into principal or independent components (PCA, ICA), combined with GSR, lead to the strongest reduction of the aforementioned effects.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the overall results of the study.

claim: Preprocessing strategies that reduce nuisance effects improve connectome-based subject identification, indicating that the high subject discriminability reported in the literature is not attributable to nuisance processes.
source: Importantly, these preprocessing strategies also improve connectome-based subject identification, indicating that the high subject discriminability reported in the literature is not attributable to nuisance processes.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the overall results of the study.

claim: The HCP dataset includes resting-state data acquired on 2 different days, during which subjects were instructed to keep their eyes open and fixated on a cross-hair.
source: The HCP dataset includes, among others, resting-state data acquired on 2 different days, during which subjects were instructed to keep their eyes open and fixated on a cross-hair.
evidence: This is a description of the dataset used in the study.

claim: Each day of HCP data collection included two consecutive 15 min resting-state runs, acquired with left-to-right (LR) and right-to-left (RL) phase encoding direction.
source: Each day included two consecutive 15 min resting-state runs, acquired with left-to-right (LR) and right-to-left (RL) phase encoding direction.
evidence: This is a description of the dataset used in the study.

claim: During each fMRI run, 1200 frames were acquired using a gradient-echo echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequence with a multiband factor of 8, spatial resolution of 2 mm isotropic voxels, and a TR of 0.72 s.
source: During each fMRI run, 1200 frames were acquired using a gradient-echo echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequence with a multiband factor of 8, spatial resolution of 2 mm isotropic voxels, and a TR of 0.72 s.
evidence: This is a description of the acquisition parameters.

claim: Cardiac and respiratory signals were measured using a standard Siemens pulse oximeter placed on the fingertip and a breathing belt placed around the chest, with a 400 Hz sampling rate.
source: Concurrently with fMRI images, cardiac and respiratory signals were measured using a standard Siemens pulse oximeter placed on the fingertip and a breathing belt placed around the chest, with a 400 Hz sampling rate.
evidence: This is a description of the physiological data acquisition.

claim: The final dataset consisted of 392 subjects.
source: The selection process resulted in a final dataset with 392 subjects (ID numbers provided in Supp. Material).
evidence: This is a description of the final sample size.
